# Cached whole-runtime LTO

Status: design for 3.0, the open questions decided by Xaymar (26 Nov 2026, see *Decisions*). Nothing of this is
implemented yet. The numbers marked *prototype* come from a Linux cloud container and only show the shape of the costs. The real numbers come
from Irkela, Shibela and merenka (see *Measurements*).

## Why

A BlitzLLVM program is the program's IR plus the runtime, which is two kinds of code today:

| Part | Lines | How it reaches the program |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The hot C parts: `runtime.c`, `runtime_objects.c`, `runtime_strings.c`, `runtime_system.c`, `banks.c` | ~2k | Shipped as source in `runtime/inline`, compiled by the user's clang together with the program (`-flto=thin`, [#104](https://github.com/Xaymar/BlitzLLVM/pull/104)) |
| Everything else, including the whole 3D scene, the renderers, 2D drawing, sound and the GUI | ~58k of C++ and ~6k of C | Prebuilt into `blitzrt.a` / `blitzrt.lib` and linked as machine code |

The second row is where the per-vertex and per-entity commands live. A loop like this one, which is what the
profile of a large user project is full of, makes one real call per command and per vertex:

```blitzbasic
For i = 0 To CountVertices(surf) - 1
	VertexNormal surf, i, nx#(i), ny#(i), nz#(i)
Next
```

Each `VertexNormal` call then does the same bookkeeping again (`code_runtime/source/scene_meshes.cpp`, `vertex_of`):

```cpp
surface* s = need_surface(handle, what);       // handle -> pointer, bounds check
if (index out of range) { bb_runtime_error(...); exit(1); }
s->dirty = true;
bb::surface_epoch++;                           // global read-modify-write
bb::surface_vertices_changed(*s);              // bound_valid = false, geometry_version++, cull_cached check, vertex_version++
```

The optimizer never sees the call and the loop together, so nothing of it is hoisted, and the increments make every
iteration depend on the one before. [#104](https://github.com/Xaymar/BlitzLLVM/pull/104) showed what the C side gains
from being compiled with the program (strings 247 → 173 ms, banks 184 → 41 ms with the IR fast paths of #94/#104). This
design does the same for the whole runtime.

## What was tried before, and why this is different

[#82](https://github.com/Xaymar/BlitzLLVM/pull/82) measured LTO with the runtime as bitcode libraries: binaries got
smaller (3.75 MB vs 4.3 MB with section GC) but a Hello World took 16–32 s to build instead of 0.6 s, already with lld,
and shipped bitcode only works with the exact LLVM version that made it. It was rejected for both reasons.

Three things change here:

1. **No shipped bitcode.** The runtime ships as source (like `runtime/inline` today) and the user's own clang compiles
   it, so there is no version to match.
2. **Compiled once, not per program.** The runtime's bitcode goes into a per-user cache, keyed by everything that
   changes it (clang, BlitzLLVM version, target, flags). A program build then only compiles the program.
3. **The ThinLTO cache.** lld keeps the machine code of every ThinLTO module it made (`--thinlto-cache-dir`) under a
   key of what went into it. A rebuild only runs the code generator for the modules whose key changed: the program's
   own, and the runtime modules whose imports, exports or liveness changed with it. The prototype below measures what
   that leaves.

The linker is not the bottleneck: with LTO, LLVM's code generation dominates the link, and that is the same work
whichever linker drives it. mold does LTO through the linker plugin API: with GCC (also MinGW under MSYS2) through
GCC's `liblto_plugin`, which reads GCC's GIMPLE bytecode, and with clang only through `LLVMgold.so`, the LLVM side of
that API, which is not there for Windows (Xaymar found that the patch for it was not merged because it would make
LLVM GPLv3). BlitzLLVM programs are LLVM IR, so the GCC route can't take them, and the clang route doesn't exist on
Windows. lld stays the linker on every platform; a faster linker would only shorten the part after code generation.

## The build of a program

```
                     once per cache key                                 every build
 runtime sources ──► clang -flto=thin -c (parallel) ──► cache/<key>/ ─┐
                                                                     ├─► clang -flto=thin -fuse-ld=lld
 program.ll ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     --thinlto-cache-dir=cache/thinlto
                                                                                    │
                                    prebuilt SDL3, SDL_image, SDL_mixer, codecs ────┘──► program
```

1. blitzcc works out the cache key (below) and looks for `<cache>/runtime/<key>/complete`.
2. If it is missing, blitzcc *prepares the runtime*: it compiles every runtime source with the flags from the manifest
   (below) into `<cache>/runtime/<key>.tmp-<pid>/`, in parallel on all cores, then renames the folder to `<key>` and
   writes `complete`. It says so once: `Preparing the runtime for clang 23.1.0 (only once): 41/96`.
3. The program is linked with the runtime's objects instead of `blitzrt.a`, between `--start-lib`/`--end-lib` so that
   only what the program needs is pulled in, as from an archive. The third-party libraries (SDL3, SDL_image, SDL_mixer
   and their codecs) and `blitzphysics` stay prebuilt; they are C behind a stable interface and are not what the hot
   loops call.
4. lld gets the ThinLTO cache (`-Wl,--thinlto-cache-dir=<cache>/thinlto` for ELF and MinGW, `-Wl,/lldltocache:` for
   lld-link) and a pruning policy (`--thinlto-cache-policy=cache_size_bytes=1g:prune_after=1209600`, two weeks).

Which runtime a build uses, from best to plainest:

| Mode | When | What is linked |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cached` | Default for optimized builds when the sources, headers and a clang with lld are there | Whole runtime from the cache, ThinLTO |
| `inline` | The cache can't be made (no C++ headers for the target, MSVC target, read-only cache, a failed prepare) | Today's path: `runtime/inline/*.c` with the program, rest prebuilt |
| `off` | `-d`, `-O0`, `--runtime-lto off` (and `--no-runtime-inline`, kept as its alias) | Prebuilt libraries only, the fastest build |

A failure falls back one row with a warning, like the inline build does today, so a broken cache never breaks a build.
`BLITZLLVM_RUNTIME_LTO=cached|inline|off` sets the default (the usual `=0` means `off`).

New options:

* `--runtime-lto <cached|inline|off>`: the mode above.
* `--prepare-runtime`: make the cache entry for the current clang and target and exit. For an IDE on its first start,
  CI, or someone who wants the one-time cost out of the way.
* `--cache-dir <dir>` / `BLITZLLVM_CACHE_DIR`: where the cache is.
* `--clear-cache`: deletes the runtime entries and the ThinLTO cache.

## What ships with BlitzLLVM

Everything that compiling the runtime needs, next to the prebuilt libraries in `lib/blitzllvm/runtime`:

* `runtime/source/`: all sources of `blitzrt` (C and C++) with their own headers, the generated `shaders.inc`,
  `shaders_opengl.inc`, `smaa.inc` and, on Windows, the D3D11 bytecode headers (`shaders_d3d11*.inc`, made by fxc at
  build time; users don't have fxc). `runtime/inline` becomes a list in the manifest instead of a copy.
* `runtime/source/manifest.txt`: written by CMake (`file(GENERATE)` from the target properties of `blitzrt`), so it
  can't drift from the real build. One line per source with its language and its own definitions
  (`process.c` has the version, `graphics_opengl.cpp` has `BB_OPENGL`, ...), and the common part: include folders
  (relative to the install), definitions, `-std=c17`/`-std=c++20`, `-fno-exceptions -fno-rtti`, `-ffp-contract=off`,
  `-ffunction-sections -fdata-sections`, and the files that must stay native code (below). It also has the SHA-256 of
  every shipped file, which goes into the cache key.
* `runtime/include/`: the headers of the libraries the runtime includes:

| Library | What is needed | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SDL3, SDL3_image, SDL3_mixer | their `include/` folders | Already installed by the dependency build, a few MB |
| Vulkan-Headers | `vulkan/` (and `vk_video/`, which `vulkan_core.h` includes) | `vulkan_core.h` alone is ~1 MB; parsed once per cache key |
| VulkanMemoryAllocator | `vk_mem_alloc.h` | ~700 KB, and `graphics_vulkan_memory.cpp` holds its implementation. One module, codegen cached |
| stb, cgltf | the single headers the runtime includes | Their implementations are compiled into one module each |
| FFmpeg, Opus | `libav*/`, `libswscale/`, `libswresample/`, `opus*.h` | Headers only, the libraries are loaded at run time |
| blitzphysics | `code_physics/include` | Only the C interface. **Jolt is not needed**: it is inside the `blitzphysics` shared library, which stays prebuilt |

The heavy headers cost time once per cache key (when the runtime is prepared), and their modules then sit in the
ThinLTO cache, because the program rarely changes what they import or export.

### Windows (llvm-mingw)

The package already ships a MinGW sysroot (`lib/blitzllvm/mingw`) with the C headers that the inline C includes,
found by scanning those sources (`cmake/install_mingw_headers.cmake`). It does not ship C++ headers. For the cached
mode it needs:

* the libc++ headers (`include/c++/v1`) of the same llvm-mingw whose `libc++.a` is shipped, so that headers and library
  match;
* the Windows headers that the C++ sources include on top (`windows.h` is already there for the C side; `d3d11.h`,
  `dxgi1_6.h`, `d3dcommon.h` and what they include). The same scan over the C++ sources finds them.

The user's clang is their own LLVM (≥ 23, see the installer decision) and the libc++ headers are those of the pinned
llvm-mingw. Newer clang with older libc++ headers is the direction that normally works, but it has to be tested with
the oldest and the newest clang we support (CI on Windows plus Irkela).

The MSVC target (`--target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`) keeps the `inline` mode: its STL and the Windows SDK are not
ours to ship, and the default Windows target is MinGW since #464.

### Linux and Flatpak

A developer build uses the system clang with the system's libstdc++ headers and glibc headers, which every clang
install already has. The Flatpak uses `org.freedesktop.Sdk.Extension.llvm21`, whose version is fixed for a given SDK.
So the Flatpak can later ship a *seed* entry: the runtime prepared by CI with exactly that clang, which blitzcc uses
(read-only) when its key matches, so Flatpak users never wait for the one-time step. If the extension updates, the key
no longer matches and the user's cache is used as everywhere else. The Flatpak's cache is
`~/.var/app/com.xaymar.BlitzLLVM/cache`, which Flatpak sets as `XDG_CACHE_HOME` by itself.

### macOS

No device and Xaymar accepts Linux plus Windows, so macOS stays on `inline` until someone tests it. The parts are the
same; Apple's linker does LTO by itself and takes `-Wl,-cache_path_lto,<dir>`.

## The cache

Where: `BLITZLLVM_CACHE_DIR`, otherwise `%LOCALAPPDATA%\BlitzLLVM\Cache` on Windows, `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/blitzllvm`
(`~/.cache/blitzllvm`) on Linux, `~/Library/Caches/BlitzLLVM` on macOS.

```
<cache>/
  runtime/
    <key>/
      key.txt          everything that went into the key, readable, for --verbose and bug reports
      deps.txt         every header the sources included (from clang -MD), with size and modification time
      objects/*.o      one ThinLTO bitcode object per source; native objects for the files below
      complete         written last: an entry without it is unfinished and gets made again
    <key>.lock         held while the entry is made
  thinlto/             lld's own cache, shared by all keys (its keys include the LLVM version and everything else)
```

### The key

SHA-256 over:

* blitzcc's version and commit, and the SHA-256 of the manifest (which has the hash of every shipped source and header);
* the clang: the full `clang --version` output, its resolved path, size and modification time (a distro rebuild of the
  same version is a different compiler), and `-print-resource-dir`;
* the target triple and the sysroot;
* every flag that changes the runtime's code: the optimization level the runtime is compiled at, `-march`/`-mcpu` and
  other target flags from `--llvm-flag`, hardening (`BLITZLLVM_HARDENING`), the allocator options.

The program's own flags (fast-math, sane evaluation order, ...) are not in it: they are written onto the program's IR,
not onto the runtime.

The system headers (libstdc++, glibc, the Windows headers of a user's own llvm-mingw) are not hashed, they are checked:
on every build blitzcc compares `deps.txt` with the files (one `stat` each, a few hundred files, about a millisecond)
and makes the entry again when one changed. This is how ccache's direct mode catches a system update without hashing
every header every time.

### Invalidation and cleanup

* A new clang, a new BlitzLLVM or other flags give a new key. Entries that were not used for 30 days are deleted at the
  next prepare, and at most four are kept (e.g. two clang versions × two targets).
* The ThinLTO cache prunes itself with the policy above.
* `--clear-cache` deletes both.

### Several builds at once

ctest runs eight compilers at once, and an IDE may build while the user does. Making an entry takes `<key>.lock` (an OS
file lock: `flock` / `LockFileEx`, released when the process dies), builds into a folder of its own and renames it. A
second blitzcc waits on the lock and then finds the entry complete. lld's ThinLTO cache is safe for parallel links by
itself (it writes to temporary files and renames them).

### Files that stay native code

Some runtime code must not go through LTO:

* `memory_interpose.c` (glibc: replaces `malloc`/`free`) and the `operator new`/`delete` of `memory.cpp`: LTO
  treats calls to library functions specially and may optimize them or drop the definitions before the linker sees that
  they are needed. They are compiled to native objects in the cache (still with the user's clang), which also keeps
  them out of the program's imports.
* Anything the manifest marks the same way later on.

## Correctness

* **Float results.** The runtime is built with `-ffp-contract=off` so that results are the same on every CPU (network
  comparisons). That stays a per-source flag in the manifest. clang then emits no `fmuladd` for runtime code, and
  inlining runtime code into the program does not give it the program's fast-math flags: those are per instruction
  (`compiler::fast_math`), and inlining keeps each instruction's own flags.
* **One definition of everything.** In `cached` mode `blitzrt.a` is not linked at all, so no symbol is defined twice.
  The inline C sources are part of the runtime there, not extra.
* **Exceptions and RTTI.** Off for the runtime as today (`-fno-exceptions -fno-rtti` in the manifest). Program IR has
  neither.
* **Crash reports.** The runtime's machine code now differs per clang. `key.txt` goes into `--verbose` output so a
  report says which compiler made it.
* **The test suite** runs in `cached` mode in CI, all of it, because LTO across the runtime can expose undefined
  behaviour in it that the prebuilt library hides. `off` and `inline` keep tests of their own (the existing
  `cli-runtime_inline` and the fallback tests of PR 4).

## Inlining is not enough: bookkeeping once per surface, not once per call

With the runtime inlined, the loop above still increments `bb::surface_epoch`, `s.geometry_version` and
`s.vertex_version` and checks `s.cull_cached` on every vertex. The increments are read-modify-writes of memory, so each
iteration waits for the previous one, and LLVM can't vectorize or hoist them. The change makes every writer store
constants instead, and moves the counting to the readers:

```cpp
// Writers (AddVertex, VertexNormal, VertexCoords, AddTriangle, ...): only stores of constants, the same every call.
s->dirty            = true;
s->bound_valid      = false;
s->pending_vertices = true;      // or pending_topology for AddVertex/AddTriangle/ClearSurface
bb::surfaces_pending = true;

// Readers (renderer, pick tree, collision, physics mesh): settle first.
inline void settle(surface& s) {
	if (s.pending_vertices | s.pending_topology) {
		s.geometry_version++;
		if (!s.pending_topology) s.vertex_version++;   // same rule as surface_vertices_changed today
		if (s.cull_cached) { s.cull_cached = false; mesh_epoch++; }
		s.pending_vertices = s.pending_topology = false;
	}
}
inline uint32_t surface_epoch_now() {
	if (surfaces_pending) { surface_epoch++; surfaces_pending = false; }
	return surface_epoch;
}
```

What the readers compare stays true: the renderer only asks whether `geometry_version` and `vertex_version` went up by
the same amount (only vertices changed), and the pick tree and collision cache only ask whether the epoch moved. Many
changes between two reads now count as one, which none of them can tell apart. Every reader of `geometry_version`,
`vertex_version`, `surface_epoch` and `bound_valid` (graphics_scene3d.cpp, collision.cpp, collision_physics.cpp,
physics_mesh.cpp, MeshWidth and the other bound queries) calls `settle` / `surface_epoch_now` first.

With constant stores the loop body has no loop-carried dependency left except the vertex data itself, and the stores
to the same addresses can be sunk out of the loop. The handle check (`need_surface`) is loop-invariant once inlined and
can be hoisted too. Whether LLVM then *vectorizes* the loop is not certain: the per-vertex index check has a cold exit
(`bb_runtime_error`), which the loop vectorizer does not handle in most loops. The goal is the removed calls and the
removed serial increments; vectorization is measured, not promised.

This change also helps the prebuilt path a little (fewer stores per call) and is its own PR, before the cache work.

## Measurements

What gets measured, per machine (Irkela and Shibela for MinGW, merenka-gpu0/1 for Linux; never Areldir), through a
coordinator slot:

| What | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Preparing the runtime (cold cache), cores used | The one-time cost a user sees after installing or updating clang |
| First build of a program after that (empty ThinLTO cache) | The cost after every BlitzLLVM or clang update |
| Rebuild, nothing changed | Floor: program codegen plus link |
| Rebuild after a one-line edit in a function body | The common case while working |
| Rebuild after using a command the program did not use before | Changes which runtime modules are live, so their ThinLTO keys |
| The same, `inline` and `off` modes | Today's baseline |
| Binary size, all three modes | #82 saw a size win from LTO |
| Run time: spacebattle (`--no-physics` too), forest 10M grass, a mesh-building loop (AddVertex/VertexNormal/VertexCoords), the string benchmark | What it buys |

Programs: Hello World, a large sample, the spacebattle and forest benchmarks, and a large user project (numbers only). If the
rebuild numbers come out much worse than the prototype's, that goes back to Xaymar before `cached` ships as the default.

### Prototype numbers (Linux cloud container, 4 cores)

Made by hand, not by blitzcc: the 93 sources of `blitzrt` compiled with the flags from `compile_commands.json` plus
`-flto=thin` (the two allocator files native), then the program's `program.ll` linked the way blitzcc does, with the
objects between `--start-lib`/`--end-lib` and `--thinlto-cache-dir`. clang 18.1.3 and lld, 4 cores, root at 2bb485f.
The scripts are not part of the repository. This only shows the shape; none of it counts as a benchmark.

| Step | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Preparing the runtime (93 files, 4 cores) | 12.8 s, 5.6 MB of bitcode |

Link of the program only (blitzcc's front end, ~0.5 s for spacebattle, comes on top in every mode):

| Program | `off` | `inline` (today) | `cached`, empty ThinLTO cache | `cached`, nothing changed | `cached`, one-line edit | `cached`, a new command |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mesh loop (below) | 0.11 s | 0.50 s | 2.90 s | 0.12 s | 0.17 s | 0.17 s (VertexColor), 2.39 s (CreateCube + RenderWorld) |
| benchmarks/spacebattle.bb | 0.46 s | 1.04 s | 4.09 s | 0.33 s | 1.03 s | 0.59 s (VertexColor) |
| benchmarks/forest.bb | 0.67 s | 1.14 s | 2.56 s | 0.36 s | | |

| Binary size | `off` | `inline` | `cached` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| spacebattle | 5.38 MB | 5.40 MB | 5.33 MB |
| forest | 5.33 MB | 5.35 MB | 5.27 MB |

Run time of the mesh loop: 200,000 vertices, 50 rounds of `VertexNormal` + `VertexCoords` on each (20 million
calls), CPU only:

| `off` | `inline` | `cached` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 80 / 83 / 83 ms | 81 / 81 / 83 ms | 34 / 35 / 34 ms |

spacebattle built in `cached` mode runs and gives the same counters as `off` (collisions, picks, hits); its frame times
on llvmpipe say nothing about the change.

What this says, to be checked on the real machines:

* The one-time step is short: about 13 s on 4 cores, so a few seconds on Irkela.
* The first link after it costs 2–4 s, far from the 16–32 s of #82. Why #82 was so much slower is not known (it may have
  used full LTO, or linked every runtime function without dead stripping); the real runs will show whether it comes back
  on Windows.
* After that, a rebuild costs about as much as today's `inline` build or less, because the ThinLTO cache also keeps the
  program's own module when it did not change. A command the program never used before pulls in its runtime modules
  once (2.4 s for the first `RenderWorld`).
* The mesh loop is 2.4 times as fast with the runtime inlined, before the bookkeeping change below.

## How it is built (PRs)

One change per PR, in this order:

1. **Bookkeeping once per surface** (`settle`, constant stores in the writers). Independent of the rest.
2. **Manifest and shipped sources**: CMake writes `manifest.txt`, installs all runtime sources, the generated shader
   headers and the third-party headers. No behaviour change.
3. **The cache in blitzcc**: key, `deps.txt` check, lock, parallel prepare, `--prepare-runtime`, `--clear-cache`,
   `--cache-dir`.
4. **Linking with the cached runtime**: `--runtime-lto`, `--start-lib`, ThinLTO cache flags, fallback chain, tests
   (cold, warm, invalidation by a fake clang, two builds at once, read-only cache falls back).
5. **Windows (MinGW)**: libc++ and the extra Windows headers in the sysroot, tested on Irkela.
6. **CI**: the whole suite in `cached` mode; the cache folder kept between runs of a job.
7. **Benchmarks** on the machines above, numbers into this document.
8. Later: the Flatpak seed entry.

## Decisions

Decided by Xaymar (26 Nov 2026):

1. **Default.** `cached` is the default for every optimized build; `inline` and `off` are the fallbacks and the
   explicit choices.
2. **Windows package size.** The libc++ headers and the extra Windows headers are always shipped; the few MB are fine.
3. **Test suite.** All of CI runs in `cached` mode.
